The bracket [SCALE, ADD] = ADD

The group commutator x⁻¹y⁻¹xy of two generators, walked on a number line, and the translation it adds up to. A picture shows a structure; it is not evidence that the structure means anything beyond its definition.

← ADD:SCALE:SIGN gallery

About this visual

What you are looking at. The group commutator [x, y] = x⁻¹y⁻¹xy of two generators, walked step by step on a number line: fire y, then x, then y⁻¹, then x⁻¹, and see where the starting point lands. Below, the translation it adds up to as the parameter moves.

How to read it. Choose a pair: (ADD, SCALE), (ADD, SIGN) or (SCALE, SIGN). Move the sliders and the start x₀. The four hops are drawn alternately above and below the line. The three start points listed under the picture all move by the same amount: the commutator is a pure translation.

What it shows. [SCALE, ADD] = ADD in the group: the commutator of ADD(a) with SCALE(s) is the translation a·(1/s − 1), of ADD(a) with SIGN(−1) the translation −2a, and SCALE with SIGN commute (the commutator is the identity). Only ADD ever appears on the right: order matters at this tier through the offset alone.

What it does not show. The Lie-algebra bracket of the same name, which is the derivative of this one at the identity. The convention x⁻¹y⁻¹xy is the one the wiki's table uses; the other convention gives the negated translation.

Numbers to check. ADD(3), SCALE(2): [ADD, SCALE] = (−1.5, 1, +1). ADD(3), SIGN(−1): [ADD, SIGN] = (−6, 1, +1). SCALE(2), SIGN(−1): identity.

Code and data. Everything shown is recomputed in the browser by ass.js (composition, inverse, commutator, word, fold, the Long Path and exact rational arithmetic) and compared with the numbers the Python engine produced (ass_data.js); the result is printed above. Light and dark follow the system.
